opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think foundation models are changing robotics in a really fundamental way. For a long time, robotics was about building very specialized systems: one model for perception, one for planning, one for control, each carefully engineered for a narrow task. The robot could be very good at one thing in one environment, but the moment you changed the lighting, the objects, or the instruction, it would fall apart.

What large foundation models bring is generality, and especially common sense about the world. A vision-language model has seen an enormous amount of human knowledge from the internet. It knows what a cup is, that you hold it by the handle, that you shouldn't put a phone in the microwave. Robots never had that kind of knowledge before. So when we connect these models to robots, the robot can suddenly understand open-ended instructions and generalize to objects and scenes it has never seen in its own training data.

At the same time, I want to be honest about what these models don't solve yet. Internet data teaches you a lot about semantics, the "what" and the "why," but much less about the "how": the physical details of contact, force, dexterity, balance. That knowledge has to come from robot experience, either real-world data or simulation, and robot data is still very scarce compared to text or images. So I see the role of foundation models as providing the brain's high-level understanding and reasoning, while a big part of our work is figuring out how to ground that in physical action, how to get the embodied data, and how to make the whole system reliable enough to actually deploy.

So I'm very optimistic. I think we're moving from robots that are programmed task by task toward robots that can learn and generalize, a bit like the transition language models went through. But the physical world is unforgiving, and closing that last gap from impressive demos to robust, everyday usefulness is where most of the hard work is now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest way to answer this is to start with what robotics looked like before these models showed up, because the contrast is really the whole story.

For most of my career, robot learning was extremely narrow. You'd pick a task, say quadruped locomotion, you'd build a simulator, you'd spend months designing reward functions and domain randomization, train a policy with reinforcement learning, and if you did everything right, the robot would walk. And then if you wanted it to open a door, you basically started over. Every skill was its own research project. The data was tiny, the generalization was poor, and nothing transferred.

What foundation models changed first wasn't the low-level control, it was the semantic layer. Suddenly a robot could be told "I spilled my drink, can you help?" and a language model could reason that this means go find a sponge, bring it over. That was what we saw with SayCan at Google. The model brought in a kind of common sense about the world that we had never been able to engineer into a robot by hand. And then with vision-language models, the robot could also look at a scene and understand it in open-ended terms rather than through a fixed set of object classes we had trained on.

The next step, which I think is the more profound one, is what people now call vision-language-action models. Instead of using the foundation model just as a planner that calls separate skills, you fine-tune it so that the output is directly the robot's actions. Projects like RT-2 showed that when you do this, the web-scale knowledge actually leaks into the physical behavior. The robot can pick up the object that corresponds to a concept it has never seen in robot data, because it learned the concept from the internet. That's the thing I find genuinely surprising, and it's why I believe the trajectory is real.

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell it. The bottleneck has moved, it hasn't disappeared. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Robots don't have an internet of actions. So the central question of the field right now is where the data comes from. Teleoperation is expensive and slow. Simulation is cheap but has a reality gap. Human video is abundant but doesn't tell you the motor commands. My view is that the answer is all of the above, and that the scaling laws we're used to in language will show up in robotics, but with a lot more engineering in the data pipeline.

The second caveat is that these models are still not great at things that require precise, fast, physical interaction. Reasoning about which cup to pick up is one thing. Actually controlling contact forces during a dexterous manipulation task, or running on uneven terrain, is a different kind of problem, and reinforcement learning and classical control still matter a lot there. I think the architecture of the future is some kind of hierarchy, where the foundation model handles understanding and high-level decisions, and lower-level controllers, often trained in simulation, handle the physics.

So if I summarize my understanding: foundation models are turning robotics from a collection of bespoke solutions into something that looks like a general learning problem. That's the biggest shift I've seen in the field. But the physical world is a harsher teacher than text, and I think the next few years are going to be about closing the gap between what the model knows and what the robot can actually do.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models will play a very important role in robotics because they bring knowledge and generalization that have been difficult to build into robots directly. A robot needs to understand what you want, recognize the objects around it, and figure out which actions might accomplish a task. Foundation models give us a powerful starting point for those capabilities.

But understanding a task and physically executing it are different problems. A model might explain how to pick up a cup, but the robot still has to decide where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and how to respond if it slips. That requires learning from interaction with the physical world and responding to feedback.

So I see foundation models working together with robot learning and control. They can help interpret instructions and plan, while the robot’s control system turns those plans into reliable actions. Over time, those capabilities may become more tightly integrated.

One of the biggest challenges is data. We have enormous amounts of text and images, but much less robot interaction data. Simulation can help, and so can learning across different robots and tasks. The exciting question is how to turn the broad knowledge in foundation models into physical skills that generalize to situations the robot hasn’t encountered before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models can play a very important role in robotics, especially in helping robots understand what people want and reason about unfamiliar situations. If you tell a robot, “Please clean up this room,” it needs to understand what that means, identify the relevant objects, and break the task into steps. Foundation models give us a powerful starting point for that kind of understanding.

But understanding a task and physically executing it are different challenges. A robot has to deal with contact, balance, uncertainty, and the consequences of its actions in real time. A model might produce a reasonable plan, but that doesn’t automatically mean the robot can carry it out reliably.

So I see a lot of promise in combining foundation models with control and learning methods that are grounded in physical interaction. The foundation model can provide high-level guidance, while the robot’s learned skills handle execution and respond to feedback. The key is closing that loop: the robot should observe whether an action worked and adjust, rather than simply follow a plan.

As these models become more capable, I expect that boundary between reasoning and control to evolve. But the measure of progress should ultimately be what a robot can do safely and reliably in the real world.
